title: Rennyo's letters
hook: the later teacher who spread Shin Buddhism through simple letters to followers

segments.voice: Yesterday, gratitude: the nembutsu in Jodo Shinshu said as thanks, not as payment. Your line was said in thanks. Who got the thank-you you usually skip? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

Evening in a farming village in Japan, long ago. The work is done, and neighbors crowd into one house. Someone unfolds a sheet of paper and reads it aloud, slowly, so the people at the back can hear. It isn't a learned treatise full of Chinese characters that only monks can follow. It's written in plain Japanese, in the simple script ordinary people could read, and it says the important thing in a few lines. When the reading ends, the room says the name together. The letter came from a teacher named Rennyo. Today: Rennyo's letters.
screen: `EVENING IN A FARMING VILLAGE.` → `A LETTER READ ALOUD.` → `PLAIN WORDS, THEN THE NAME.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. Rennyo came generations after Shinran, a descendant who became head of the Honganji, the temple that grew from Shinran's grave. Tradition remembers him as the teacher who carried Shin Buddhism out of a small circle and into villages across Japan. Second, his tool: the letter. Rennyo wrote to followers in plain Japanese, using the simple script, not the dense Chinese of scholars. Tradition says his letters were copied by hand, carried from village to village, and read aloud in gatherings. Shin Buddhists still read them in services; one branch calls them Ofumi, the letters, and another Gobunsho. Third, what the letters keep saying. Again and again they come back to a short core, close to everything this week has covered. Entrust yourself to Amida with a single heart, let go of trying to earn your way, and then say the name in thanks. He didn't add new layers. He kept taking layers off. Fourth, the letter people know best. It's often called the letter on white ashes. It says, in effect: in the morning we may have rosy cheeks, and by evening be white ashes. Life is that short and that uncertain, so don't put off the one thing that matters. It is read aloud at Shin funerals. Rennyo's gift was not a new idea. It was plainness: saying the deep thing in words a tired farmer could hear after dark, and remember the next morning.
screen: `A LATER HEAD OF THE HONGANJI.` · `LETTERS IN PLAIN JAPANESE.` · `ENTRUST, THEN SAY THE NAME IN THANKS.` · `MORNING CHEEKS, EVENING ASHES.` · then, large: `SIMPLE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a simple letter, in your head for now. Settle, and breathe. Choose one person who might need to hear something from you. Now compose it in as few words as you can: who it's to, the one thing you want them to know, and your name. No explaining, no extra layers. Say it over a few times until it's plain enough to read aloud in a dim room. If you have paper nearby, you can write it down after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Rennyo's letters. Short letters in plain Japanese that carried Shinran's teaching to ordinary people, still read aloud in Shin services. Today's word.
Your line: simple letters. Today, send the letter you composed, as a text, a card or a note, and keep it short enough to read in one breath. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

screen: `DAY 1268 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CHAN AND PURE LAND TOGETHER.`

notes: No generation count or dates given for Rennyo; 'a descendant who became head of the Honganji, the temple that grew from Shinran's grave' (the Otani mausoleum): confirm.
Ofumi (Otani-ha usage) and Gobunsho (Hongwanji-ha usage): confirm the branch naming.
The white-ashes letter (Hakkotsu no Gobunsho) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm that it is commonly read at Shin funerals ('often' used).
'Tradition remembers him as the teacher who carried Shin Buddhism out of a small circle and into villages': confirm fair.
Hook scene (a village gathering reading a letter) is illustrative of the ko gatherings; confirm.
